title: The Rich Merchant and His Sons
summary: A dying merchant asks Akbar to choose which of his three sons should inherit his estate. Birbal gives each son one copper coin to fill a room.
keywords: the rich merchant and his sons
full_text:
A wealthy silk merchant of Agra named Seth Dhaniram approached Emperor Akbar with an unusual petition. Feeling his health failing, Dhaniram explained:

'Your Majesty, I have amassed a fortune of three hundred thousand gold mohurs. I have three grown sons, but I do not know which one possesses the wisdom to preserve my family name. If I divide the fortune equally, a foolish son will squander his share on gambling and bring ruin to all. I beg your royal court to test my sons and name the rightful custodian.'

Akbar turned to Birbal, who agreed to conduct a test.

Birbal summoned the three young men to the palace courtyard. He handed each brother an identical single copper dam (the smallest coin in the empire) and said:

'Here is your trial. Each of you must take this single copper coin to the bazaar. You must buy something with it that will completely fill this entire empty banquet hall from wall to wall and floor to ceiling before sunset. He who succeeds shall inherit his father's entire estate.'

The eldest son hurried to the bazaar, laughing: 'A single copper coin to fill a palace hall? It is impossible! But let me buy the cheapest bulk goods available.' He bought five cartloads of foul-smelling straw and dumped it in the hall. The straw filled only a corner, creating a dusty, sneezing mess.

The second son shook his head: 'Straw is too expensive.' He went to the riverbanks, bought three cartloads of dry autumn leaves, and dumped them inside. The leaves filled only half the floor, blowing everywhere when the wind blew through the archways.

Finally, the youngest son arrived just as the sun dipped beneath the horizon. He carried nothing but a small clay oil lamp and a single sweet-smelling stick of incense, which he had bought for his copper coin.

He placed the lamp in the center of the dark, cavernous hall and struck a flint. Instantly, radiant golden light filled every square inch of the hall, banishing the darkness from wall to wall and ceiling to floor, while the fragrant smoke of the incense filled the air with sweetness!

Birbal smiled proudly: 'Behold, Your Majesty. Folly fills a house with dust and clutter. But wisdom, like light and virtue, requires very little material wealth to illuminate an entire home and bless all who dwell within.'

Akbar and Dhaniram joyfully declared the youngest son the chief heir, teaching the older brothers that intellect is greater than brute accumulation.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Rich Merchant and His Sons"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
